prompt.context: Your client is the owner of UPS #88, a racecar on the NASCAR tour. It races in the Nextel Cup, a points-based championship where the season winner has accumulated the most points over the course of the racing season. There are 36 races in total, running from February to November. Dale Jarrett, a well-known celebrity driver, races for the team. Dale helped win the Nextel Cup three years ago, and so far this year is eighth in a field of 43 drivers. A close friend who is the VP of marketing at Home Depot recently contacted the client. She inquired about sponsoring a second racing team with the client. She recognizes that NASCAR is the fastest growing segment among males ages 18-45. She also has talked to a successful driver from a regional drag racing circuit to try out as the driver of the team.
prompt.question: Evaluate the potential of this opportunity.

clarifying_info.q: What are the sources of revenue for the current team?
clarifying_info.a: See Exhibit 1 — revenue sources include Sponsorships (60%), Nextel Cup Race Winnings (25%), Selling Engines (10%), and Merchandising (5%).

clarifying_info.q: What are the cost components for the current team?
clarifying_info.a: See Exhibit 2 — costs include Salary (40%), Equipment (25%), Travel (5%), Lease/engine shop (10%), and R&D (20%). Total costs are $20M.

clarifying_info.q: How much are race winnings per race?
clarifying_info.a: Winnings range from $50K to $1MM per race depending on finishing position and race significance.

clarifying_info.q: How many races does the driver qualify for?
clarifying_info.a: Assume the driver qualifies for 30 of the 36 races.

exhibits.title: Revenue Sources
exhibits.shows: A table listing the four revenue streams for the current team, each with a percentage of total revenues and a brief description.

data.Sponsorships: 60% — UPS dominates; other sponsors include Outback Steakhouse and 3M
data.Nextel Cup Race Winnings: 25% — $50K to $1MM per race depending on finishing position and race significance
data.Selling Engines: 10% — Strong R&D shop; engines sold to professional drivers domestically
data.Merchandising: 5% — Licensed to third-party; T-shirts and caps

exhibits.title: Cost Sources
exhibits.shows: A table listing the five cost categories for the current team, each with a percentage of total costs and a brief description.

data.Salary: 40% — Race-facing 50% (mechanics and Dale Jarrett); non race-facing 50% (engine shop technicians, HR, accounting)
data.Lease, engine shop: 10% — Leasing of land in rural North Carolina

framework: Profitability of the existing team (baseline revenue and cost structure)
Incremental cost of adding a second team (marginal cost analysis)
Revenue potential of the new Home Depot–sponsored team
Minimum sponsorship fee to charge Home Depot (break-even on marginal costs)
Strategic and risk considerations (driver quality, resource dilution, bargaining power)

questions.prompt: What is the total annual revenue of the existing team?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use race winnings (25% of revenue) as the anchor. Estimate average winnings per race, multiply by races qualified, then gross up using the 25% share. A reasonable average is $200K/race.

math.setup: Race winnings = avg winnings per race × races qualified. Race winnings = 25% of total revenue, so total revenue = race winnings / 0.25.
math.answer: Total revenue ≈ $24M (assumption-dependent; interviewer should check that assumed average yields a plausible profit)

questions.prompt: What is the profit of the existing team?
questions.guidance: Subtract total costs from total revenue. Total costs are given as $20M once the candidate has outlined cost buckets from Exhibit 2.

steps: Total costs = $20M (given after cost buckets outlined)

questions.prompt: What is the minimum amount the client should charge Home Depot for the sponsorship (i.e., the marginal cost of adding the new team)?
questions.guidance: Identify which cost components are affected by adding a second team. Salary (race-facing half only), Equipment, and Travel will double; Lease and R&D are tied to the engine shop and do not change. Calculate each incremental cost and sum them.

math.setup: Race-facing salary = 50% of salary cost. Each of race-facing salary, equipment, and travel doubles, so the incremental cost equals the current cost of each affected line.
math.answer: Minimum sponsorship fee = $10M (marginal cost of the new team)

questions.prompt: Should the client charge a premium above $10M to Home Depot? Why or why not?
questions.guidance: No single right answer; evaluate the candidate's reasoning. Arguments for a premium: Home Depot has already begun negotiations with a driver, signaling commitment and giving the client bargaining power; Home Depot can receive an ROI analysis justifying the premium through brand exposure to fast-growing 18–45 male demographic. Arguments against a premium: Home Depot has outside options — sponsoring a different NASCAR team, a different sport (e.g., baseball), or a different racing circuit (e.g., Formula One).

brainstorming.prompt: What are the risks and strategic considerations of adding the new Home Depot team?

categories.name: Driver quality and experience
ideas: New driver has only drag racing experience, not oval-track NASCAR experience
Drag racing driver lacks name recognition, reducing merchandising revenue potential
Lower performance likely in initial seasons

categories.name: Resource dilution
ideas: High-quality mechanics from Dale Jarrett's team may be reassigned to the new team
Dilutes performance and results of the flagship #88 car
Management bandwidth spread across two teams

categories.name: Cost assumptions validity
ideas: New driver's salary may be lower than average due to lack of name recognition — could reduce marginal salary cost
Total equipment cost may be lower than average due to leveraging existing engine shop technology
Engine shop closure not recommended without margin data to support it

categories.name: Sponsorship and revenue upside
ideas: Home Depot brings large, credible corporate sponsor with strong brand
Diversifies revenue away from UPS concentration
NASCAR's fastest-growing male 18–45 demographic aligns with Home Depot customer base

categories.name: Strategic fit
ideas: Running two teams adds operational complexity
Brand association risk if new team performs poorly
Opportunity to scale engine-selling business with second team's R&D data

recommendation: Pursue the Home Depot sponsorship opportunity — the existing team is profitable ($4M), and marginal costs of the new team ($10M) can be fully covered by the Home Depot sponsorship fee
Set the minimum sponsorship ask at $10M; consider charging a premium given Home Depot's demonstrated commitment and the demographic appeal of NASCAR to their target customer
risks: New drag-racing driver has unproven NASCAR oval-track skills, risking poor performance
Resource dilution may hurt Dale Jarrett's flagship team results
Merchandising revenue from new team will be limited by driver's anonymity
recommendation.risks_note: Risks should be disclosed to Home Depot and factored into contract terms (e.g., performance milestones).
next_steps: Negotiate sponsorship contract with Home Depot with a floor of $10M and performance incentives
Assess new driver's readiness through qualifying races or test sessions before committing
Define resource-sharing protocols to protect the flagship Dale Jarrett team's performance
